en: Saying “I entrust myself to God,” girding my waist,
Standing and struggling for the standard,
For my kin, against these dogs,
I will enter battle without delay.
I will raise a terrible slaughter;
My horses taken by the Chinese,
I will wrest them free,’ he said.
Clothed in white armor,
If you were to look at Manas,
He raged like a white tiger.
He had donned his white armor;
He had mounted Toruchaar.
His eyes blazed like fire;
His thirst for blood had seized him.
His white teeth were like a gate,
Teeth unlike other people's;
They jutted out gleaming white.
His anger rose and burst forth.
If you looked at every limb,
He seemed like a lion.
Raging, the valiant one,
His form and figure,
His appearance mounted on his horse,
When one looked, he appeared to the eye
Like a thousand men.
The man, the leopard supported by Shay,
The youngest of six lions,
Allah's beloved servant—
His world was in balance;
He was the lion supported by Shay.
If you looked within him,
He was broader than the face of the earth.
No one who faced him remained alive;
No man dared go against him.
He was one of the marked lions;
He was the valiant lion Manas.
His protectors were one nine;
On that day, Manas
Had come under their protection.
The black-spotted leopard,
When he headed toward the enemy,
Raged at his flank.
The short-tailed, gray-maned lion,
Companion to the hero,
Raged behind him.
The forty chiltens and Kydyr Niyaz,
Companions to the hero,
All shouted encouragement,
Shouting encouragement to Manas.
No mortal could bring him harm;
Whoever came against him face to face
Could not survive alive.
His world was in balance;
If you looked within him,
He was broader than the face of the earth.
Created with surpassing fortune,
He was the lion Bloodthirsty Manas.
Holding a people, governing a country,
He had the bearing of a leader.
Leading a people, governing a country,
He had the bearing of a champion.
To raise turmoil throughout the world—
He showed the bearing of one who could.
Entering alone and smashing through,
Beijing with its seven gates—
He showed the bearing of one who could take it.
He mounted in wrath;
Against the lion himself
A doomed man would come.
If you saw the hero's form,
He was like a fortress built of iron.
Not only Kochku—if he attacked,
Even Esenkan could not survive.
High-browed, fierce in menace,
He would lay flat whoever challenged him.
Wide-mouthed, cliff-browed,
His face like oiled wheat,
His eyes like dusk and mist,
Rich Jakyp's young Manas
Girded his full-grown waist,
Struck Toruchaar once on the thigh,
Took his lacquered spear in hand
And roared in wrath.
Behind him, forty children
Cried the battle cry ‘Manas!’
Making a road through roadless land,
Valiant Manas the leopard
Then attacked Kochku
And the seven hundred under him.
Their very center, mighty Manas,
Who was twelve at that time,
Came and tore through it.
The forty children came to their very middle
And closed in upon it.
Through their center your mighty one
Went tearing his way out.
Toruchaar beneath him,
When he heard shouting, surged forth.
When the uproar rose, the noble beast
Showed the bearing of a tulpar.
Unflustered when he heard shouting,
In the darkness of the moon,
He never misplaced a single step.
Surging forth when he heard uproar,
Toruchaar beneath him
Showed the bearing of a tulpar.
When he galloped, the black earth
Split apart layer by layer.
He did not slip on the heights;
He was in no way inferior
To a wild goat treading stone.
Ridden into combat, he did not falter;
Ridden into battle, he did not tire;
Ridden with the baggage train, he did not flag.
Hoe-hoofed, broad-rumped,
The tulpar of spacious lands,
A hardy, well-bred horse,
Sieve-lunged, copper-limbed,
Khan Manas's Toruchaar,
Growing wild and straining,
When he entered combat,
He bucked as if his rider had died.
The stones he trod shattered;
Clods as large as a traveling hut,
Above wolf-maned Manas the tiger,
Whistled overhead.
His flesh stood out like a sheep's;
His back straightened like a hare's.
His mouth opened like a chasm;
White foam mixed with blood
Splashed upon his chest.
Making him rear and strain,
The hero Manas entered combat,
Surging forward with Toruchaar.
The socketed lacquered spear
He raised high, looming above.
Before the enemy striking at him,
He did not open his guard in fear.
The men who struck at him,
He stamped into the ground like hares.
He moistened his spear with blood.
The champions who came to shoot
He pressed to the ground like hares.
When they had raided the horses,
When the first shout rose,
There had been seven hundred champions.
When he attacked with a shout,
Nothing of them remained.
When Manas lunged to attack,
Twelve champions fell.
Their mail-clad champions
Lay dead, stretched out.
Their jacket-wearing champions
Lay dead, sprawled out.
The renowned died, people died;
Their champions numbered seven hundred.
All whom he met died;
All the havoc was stilled;
All the horses were gathered.
Manas the mighty leopard,
When he lunged again and again,
Twelve champions lay stretched out.
When the mighty one attacked,
All who faced him
Fell from their horses, stretched out.
Before one could say this or that,
Before an eye could blink,
He began the turmoil.
Their champions numbered seven hundred;
Your accomplished Bloodthirsty Manas
Reached them and slaughtered them all.
Their champion hero Kochku,
To raise a struggle,
To spear young Manas,
To stir up trouble,
That bastard turned his thoughts
Toward Esenkan's presence,
To take Manas there bound.
Fire burned throughout his innards.
Taking his true spear in hand,
Striking his pure chestnut once,
Roaring in wrath,
Crying the battle cry ‘Möndü!’
His blue-gray coat of armor showed.
Those who saw him were troubled;
When your unbeliever raged,
He appeared like Ala-Too.
That Kochku who came
Had a head like a great cauldron,
His brows were like reclining dogs.
If you looked at his mustache,
It was like nettles grown on old dung.
Look at the grime on his smoking pipe:
Like ground grain smeared about by children eating.
The tuft of hair down his back
Was like a stallion's mane.
The champion Kochku was a warrior;
From the presence of Esenkan,
Vowing, “I will bring Manas bound,”
He had set out with menace.
He, too, would never give up wrestling;
The flesh of a whole pig
Could not fill him at one sitting.
A trick rider, a swift runner on foot,
An honored, mighty champion,
His eyes were like the mouth of a grave,
As though they could suck in all they saw.
The nostrils of his nose
Were like winding gullies and ravines.
Whoever Kochku met,
He seemed ready to swallow, horse and all.
Do not ask about this Kochku:
He had the look of a thousand champions.
Could any mortal bring him low?
Could anyone meet him and survive?
His father was a raging Chinese brute;
Unable to understand human speech,
He was a beast-like swine.
Angry with Manas,
He loomed in his fury,
Huge and towering as a mountain:
“You have reached the age of twelve;
Even if you were eighty Manases,
Today you would die by my hand.
I will finish all of you together,
Beginning with your father, wealthy Jakyp.
I will bind you all and take you away.
Root and branch, you wretched Buruts,
I will finish all of you together.
When we merely played, you Burut,
You began this furious turmoil.
I had seven hundred champions;
You slaughtered every one.
My anger has risen; I stand unyielding.
Now I will put an end to you.
I will drive your caravan out of Altai,
You fucking, wretched Burut!
Now I will take my revenge.
Even if you had forty-five lives,
You fucker, I would spare none.”
Raging and thundering,
The infidel gathered his strength;
The ground split with the pounding.
Warrior Kochku came out for single combat,
The hair on his crown bristling.
Summoning his strength, straining forward,
To lay hands on Manas,
Kochku stood ready.
At that moment Khan Manas,
Born to surpassing good fortune,
Struck Toruchaar once on the flank.
“Let fate decide!” your warrior cried,
Taking his lacquered spear in hand.
His back hunched behind him,
His ribs stood out one by one;
The sight of him seized the heart.
